v.why: Raising an already huge learning rate (0.08 to 1) causes divergence or dead ReLUs, whereas at other bands the same step is less harmful.
At very small learning rates the network is undertrained after 243 epochs, so a larger step helps much more than elsewhere.
With a tiny learning rate, a larger batch means fewer updates, so the network is even more undertrained.
Larger batches give less noisy gradients, which stabilizes training at very high learning rates.
Wider layers make the effective update size larger, so they destabilize training further at high learning rates.
Wider networks move further per Adam step, which speeds up learning when the learning rate is tiny.
Deeper networks are more prone to divergence and dead units at high learning rates.
Pushing the L2 penalty toward 1 over-regularizes and underfits, while increases at small alpha have almost no effect.
Narrow networks have little spare capacity, so stronger L2 hurts them more than wide networks.
Small batches with very high learning rates give noisy, unstable updates that hurt accuracy.

I did not run any experiments or look at the data. These ten hypotheses come from reasoning about how Adam training of ReLU MLPs behaves, so they are my best judgement and are untested.

The main ideas:
- Very high learning rates make training unstable.
- Very low learning rates leave the network undertrained.
- Larger batches mean fewer updates in the same number of epochs.
- Strong L2 penalties hurt most when the network is small.
